drafts.p0:control:
Slow queries usually aren't a database choice problem—they're a schema or query problem. Switching to Mongo won't fix them; you'll just hit different limits.

What's actually slow? If you're doing N+1 queries or scanning huge tables without indexes, Postgres can handle that fine once you fix it. If your schema has joins that are awkward, that's a real Postgres friction point—but it's fixable with denormalization or materialized views. Mongo trades write complexity for read speed on nested data, but it costs you elsewhere: transactions are messier, aggregations get verbose, and you lose the safety rails.

Before you migrate, profile a few of those slow queries. What are they doing—full table scans, complex joins, sorting on unindexed columns? Once you know the actual bottleneck, the right fix is usually clearer than switching databases entire. If it's join-heavy work on nested structures, Mongo's worth reconsidering. If it's index tuning, you're already there.
drafts.p0:constraint-hardness-testing:
Slow queries usually aren't a database problem — they're a query problem. Before you switch databases, figure out what's actually happening.

Start with the basics: are you indexing the columns you filter and join on? A missing index on a frequently-queried field will make any database crawl. Check your query plans — Postgres has `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which shows exactly where the time goes. If you're seeing sequential scans on large tables, that's your answer.

Next, look at your schema. Are you normalizing things that shouldn't be normalized, or denormalizing things that should be? Running a query that joins six tables together will be slow in Postgres *and* Mongo. Switching databases won't fix a schema that's fighting you.

The real question before you switch is: have you actually hit a limit that Postgres can't handle? Postgres handles millions of rows and complex queries well. It's not fast because you didn't tune it — and tuning is cheaper than rewriting everything. Mongo's strength is different — flexible documents, horizontal scaling, eventual consistency — not speed on the queries you're probably running.

What kind of queries are slow? Are we talking joining across tables, or filtering and sorting on a single collection?
drafts.p0:creativity-assumption-excavator:
Before you jump databases, it's worth asking what's actually slow and why. Postgres hits performance walls usually because of missing indexes, poorly written queries, or a schema that wasn't built for your access patterns — not because it's the wrong database. Have you run an explain plan on the slow queries to see where the time's going?

The assumption underneath the switch is often that a different database will fix it, but you'd likely carry the same problems over. Mongo shines when you're working with deeply nested or highly variable data shapes, not when you've got relational queries that are just unoptimized. If your slow queries are joins, aggregations, or filtering on unindexed columns, those exist in Mongo too — they just look different and feel less familiar when you're debugging them.

What does your schema look like, and what kind of queries are timing out? That'll tell you whether Postgres is actually the bottleneck or whether it's the tuning.
drafts.p0:decision-premortem-analysis:
I'd flip this around: imagine you've made the switch and it's six months later. What went wrong?

Usually it's one of three things. First, the slow queries weren't actually the database's fault — they were missing indexes, N+1 queries in your code, or a schema that didn't fit your access patterns. You switch databases and the same problems follow you because the real issue lives in the application layer, not the storage layer. Second, you've now got operational debt: Mongo handles transactions differently, backups work differently, your team needs different skills. The migration cost was real; the performance gain wasn't big enough to justify it. Third, you picked the wrong tool for the data shape — Postgres is actually better for what you're storing, and now you're fighting the database instead of working with it.

Before you switch, profile the slow queries. Find out *why* they're slow: is it a missing index, a join that's doing work it shouldn't, or a query that's fundamentally expensive? That answer tells you whether swapping databases will actually help. If it's index-related or query-shaped, Postgres will be fine once you fix it. If it's truly about the data model — you're storing deeply nested documents and constantly unpacking them — then maybe Mongo fits better. But most of the time, the database isn't the bottleneck.

What do the slow queries actually look like?
drafts.p0:investigation-counter-hypothesis:
Before you switch, let's check whether the database itself is actually the bottleneck. Slow queries usually mean one of three things, and only one of them is "the database can't handle this data."

First: are the queries poorly written? Missing indexes, N+1 loops, or fetching way more data than you need will tank performance on any database. Postgres has tools — EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows exactly where time goes — that can surface this fast. If you're not using those yet, that's the first move.

Second: is your data model fighting the schema? Postgres works best with normalized, relational data. If you're storing deeply nested documents or constantly reshaping rows into objects, you're swimming upstream. That *could* point toward Mongo. But it could also point toward rethinking the queries or the schema itself — sometimes normalizing better actually speeds things up.

Third: are you actually at scale? Mongo's real advantage appears when you have massive write volume or genuinely unstructured data. If you've got, say, fifty thousand rows and a few slow queries, Mongo won't fix it — a better index will.

The honest thing: switching databases is expensive. You'll rewrite the data layer, retrain your intuitions, and pick up Mongo's own pitfalls (transactions were rough for years, distributed joins don't exist the same way). If slow queries are the problem, the database usually isn't the real answer.

What does your slowest query look like, and how much data are we talking about?

Start with: what exactly happens when someone tries to log in now? Does it error out, redirect somewhere unexpected, hang, or silently fail? And do you know what was in this deploy — schema changes, authentication logic, environment variables, API endpoints?

Also worth checking: did the break happen immediately after deploy, or did it surface later? And is it affecting everyone or specific users or conditions?

drafts.p3:creativity-assumption-excavator:

The reason I'm asking is that deploy-and-break can mean a few different things depending on timing. Sometimes it's genuinely the code change. Sometimes it's a configuration that didn't propagate, or a database migration that only affects certain environments, or even a timing issue where something worked in staging because the data was different. And sometimes the breakage was already there — login's just the flow that happened to expose it first.

What does "break" look like from the user side? Are they getting an error, a redirect loop, a timeout, or does the page just sit there?
drafts.p3:decision-premortem-analysis:
Let me work backwards from what went wrong. A login flow breaks after deploy usually for a few reasons, and the most common ones cluster around a few areas.

If the authentication service didn't get updated alongside the client code, you've got a version mismatch — the frontend's expecting a response shape the backend isn't sending anymore. Same problem happens when environment variables didn't propagate, so the service is pointing at the wrong database or auth provider.

Session handling is another frequent culprit. If you changed how tokens are stored, validated, or refreshed — even small changes to the payload or expiry logic — existing sessions break, or new ones won't create. And if the deploy rolled out unevenly across load-balanced instances, some servers might be running the old code while others run the new, which looks like an intermittent bug.

The third category is dependency or configuration drift. A new package version with a breaking change, a middleware order shuffle, or a CORS policy that got stricter without you realizing it — these all hit the login path hard because it's one of the first things that runs.

What would help narrow it down: is the break complete — login doesn't work at all — or intermittent? And did anything change server-side in this deploy, or just client code?
drafts.p3:investigation-counter-hypothesis:
I'd need to see what changed in the deploy to tell you for sure, but here's what I'd check first. The login flow usually breaks at one of three points: the frontend can't reach the auth endpoint, the endpoint exists but returns something unexpected, or the response shape changed. Start by checking your network tab — are the auth requests even going out, and what status codes are you seeing?

If those look fine, compare what the auth service is actually returning now versus what your frontend expects. Schema changes are sneaky — maybe a field got renamed, wrapped in an object, or started coming back as null. What did you change in this deploy? Frontend, backend, both?
